before: Zebulun was a people who risked their lives to death, and Naphtali too, on the heights of the field.
after: Zebulun was a people who risked their lives even to death, and Naphtali too, on the heights of the field.
rationale: Add even to make the English degree expression intelligible while retaining the source’s life/death language and the parallel naming of Zebulun and Naphtali; preserve poetry.
tsw_comparator: Zebulun was a people who risked their lives to death, and Naphtali also, on the heights of the field.

before: Through the window Sisera’s mother looked, crying through the lattice: “Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why are the hoofbeats of his chariots delayed?”
after: Through the window Sisera’s mother looked, crying through the lattice: “Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why is the clatter of his chariots delayed?”
rationale: Render the figurative footsteps of the chariots as clatter rather than assigning hooves to the vehicles. Retain both questions, the mother’s waiting, and poetic lines; explain the footsteps image in a selective note.
tsw_comparator: Through the window she looked down, the mother of Sisera cried through the lattice: “Why is his chariot delayed in coming? Why are the hoofbeats of his chariots late?”

before: Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart. She sent for the Philistine rulers: “Come up this time. He has told me all his heart.” They came to her with the silver in their hands.
after: Delilah saw that he had told her all that was in his heart. She sent for the Philistine rulers: “Come up this time. He has told me all that is in his heart.” They came to her with the silver in their hands.
rationale: Use the same natural full-heart-disclosure construction as verse 17, preserving both repetitions in 18 and the read-tradition me; do not replace heart with an abstract secret.
tsw_comparator: When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called the rulers of the Philistines, saying, “Come up this time, for he has told me all his heart.” Then the rulers of the Philistines came up to her and brought the silver in their hands.

before: On the fifth day he rose early to leave. The woman’s father said, “Please strengthen yourself.” They lingered until the day began to decline, and the two men ate.
after: On the fifth day he rose early to leave. The woman’s father said, “Please strengthen yourself. Stay until the day begins to decline.” The two men ate.
rationale: Keep the plural imperative vehitmahmehu inside the father’s speech. The prior draft changed his request into narrated action. Preserve the fifth day, declining daylight and the two men eating; a note explains the plural address.
tsw_comparator: He rose early in the morning on the fifth day to go, but the young woman’s father said, “Please strengthen your heart and remain until the day declines.” So the two of them ate.

before: The men would not listen to him. Then the man seized his concubine and brought her out to them. They raped her and abused her all night until morning, and let her go as dawn was breaking.
after: The men would not listen to him. Then her husband seized his concubine and brought her out to them. They raped her and abused her all night until morning, and let her go as dawn was breaking.
rationale: Identify the man who seizes his own concubine as her husband, already identified in 19:3. This distinguishes his action from the host’s preceding offer and preserves the assault, abuse and dawn release without resolving her time of death.
tsw_comparator: But the men would not listen to him. So the man seized his concubine and brought her out to them. They knew her and abused her all night until morning, and they released her when the dawn began to rise.
